title: A Volleyball Team Gets Ready
summary: We learn be going to, will, have to and must with a volleyball team.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: We learn be going to, will, have to and must. Today we follow a volleyball team as it gets ready for a big game. After each part, you play a practice game.

items.prompt: What are you going to do after school today?
Do you play on a team? What rules do you follow at practice?
Have you watched Haikyuu? Which player would you like to be?

blocks.title: Part 1: Be Going To for Team Plans
paragraphs: There is a volleyball team at Riverside High School. The team has a big game in two weeks.
Use be going to for a plan you made before you speak. The form is am, is or are, then going to, then the base form. The base form is the dictionary form of a verb: play, practice, serve.
- I am going to play. Short form: I'm going to play.
- She is going to play. Short form: She's going to play.
- We are going to play. Short form: We're going to play.
- Not: Leo is not going to play.
- To ask: Are you going to play? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Coach Carter has eleven players. But a volleyball team has only six players on the court at one time. So she is going to choose six players for the first game.

The team is also going to practice rotation. In volleyball, players rotate. They move one place on the court. They go the same way as the hands of a clock. They do this when their team wins the serve from the other team. For example, the other team serves, and our team wins the point. Now it is our turn to serve, so our players rotate. Why? After each rotation, a different player serves.
Look at these examples.
1. We are going to practice every day after school.
2. Coach Carter is going to choose six players for the first game.
3. Mia is going to practice her serve on Saturday morning.
4. Leo is not going to play this week. He hurt his hand.

images.alt: A woman coach in a tracksuit holds a clipboard and talks to six boys and girls on an indoor school volleyball court before practice. The players wear navy shirts with white trim, navy shorts and knee pads, and each stands in their own place on the court.

items.explanation: After going to, use the base form, like play.

items.explanation: For a plan made before you speak, use we are going to and the base form.

items.explanation: After going to, use the base form, so choose and not chooses.

blocks.title: Part 2: Will for Quick Choices
paragraphs: In a game, there is often no time to plan. Then we use will.
Will + the base form talks about the future. Will is the same for every person: I will, she will, they will. The short forms are I'll, she'll and they'll. The not form is will not, or won't.
We use will in three ways.
- For a choice you make right now, at the moment you speak.
- For an offer or a promise: I'll help you.
- When you think something will happen: I think we will win.

Be going to and will both talk about the future. For plans and choices, the difference is when you decide. Mia decided last week, so she says: I am going to practice on Saturday. But in a game, the ball flies fast to Leo. He has no time to plan. He decides now and shouts: I'll get it!
For what you think will happen, both are OK. I think we will win. I think we are going to win.

Quick choices are very important in volleyball. Why? A rally starts with the serve. It ends when the ball is out of play. This happens when the ball hits the floor, or when a player breaks a rule. Then the referee blows a whistle. This shows that the rally has ended. The team that wins the rally gets one point. This is true even if the other team served. So every ball is important.
A volleyball game has up to five sets. A set is one part of the game, with its own points. The team that wins three sets wins the game.
Look at these examples.
1. The ball is coming to me. I'll get it!
2. Your bag looks heavy. I'll carry it for you.
3. I will serve well tomorrow. I promise.
4. It's 24–24. I think we will win this set.
5. Don't worry, Coach. We won't give up.

images.alt: A teenage boy in the team's navy shirt and shorts runs and dives low for a fast ball in a bright school gym, shouting with his mouth open as he reaches for it. A girl teammate in the same navy kit steps back to leave the ball to him.

items.explanation: When you decide right now, at the moment you speak, use will.

items.prompt: Mia made a plan last week. Now she tells Leo: I ___ practice on Saturday.
items.explanation: For a plan made before you speak, use be going to.

pairs: I will serve well. I promise.
items.explanation: We use will for a choice made now, an offer, a promise and what you think will happen.

items.sourceJa: 私たちはあきらめません。
items.explanation: Won't is the short form of will not, and the base form comes after it.
After will, use the base form, so serve and not serves.

items.prompt: It's 24–24. I think we ___ win this set.
items.hint: Words for what you think about later.
items.explanation: When you think something will happen, use I think with will.
The not form of will is will not, or won't.

blocks.title: Part 3: Have To for Game Rules
paragraphs: Before the big game, Coach Carter explains the game rules.
Have to + the base form says that something is necessary. The reason often comes from outside you: a rule, a teacher or a coach.
- I, you, we, they: have to.
- He, she, it: has to.
- The past, for every person: had to.
- To ask: Do we have to practice? Does she have to serve?
- Not: don't have to, doesn't have to. It is not necessary. You can do it, but you don't need to.
Before each serve, the referee blows a whistle. Then the player who serves has to hit the ball within 8 seconds. Why? This way, the game does not stop for long.

Many people think players have to use their hands. They don't have to! After the serve, players can hit the ball with any part of the body. Even a leg is OK. So when a ball flies low, Leo can save it with his leg.
Look at these examples.
1. Mia has to serve within 8 seconds.
2. We have to practice hard before the big game.
3. Leo had to stay home yesterday. He was sick.
4. You don't have to use your hands. A leg is OK too.
5. Do we have to practice on Sunday? No, you don't have to.

images.alt: Inside a bright school gym with a wooden floor, a referee stands on a tall referee's stand at one end of the net with a whistle in his mouth. A player in the team's navy shirt and shorts stands just behind the end line, holding the ball and ready to serve.

blocks.title: Part 4: Must and Must Not on the Court
paragraphs: Some rules on the court are very strong. For these rules, we often use must and must not.
Must + the base form says that something is very important or necessary. Must is the same for every person: I must, he must, they must. Must not, or mustn't, says that something is not allowed.

Must and have to are close in meaning. Must often shows the speaker's own strong feeling. Coach Carter says: You must sleep early tonight! That is her own idea. Have to often talks about a rule from outside. But rule books also use must for very strong rules. Also, must has no past form. For the past, use had to: We had to practice on Sunday.
Must not and don't have to are very different.
- You must not catch the ball. It is not allowed.
- You don't have to jump for every ball. It is not necessary. You can choose.
In a rally, players must not catch the ball. They must hit it. If a player catches the ball, the other team gets one point.
Players must have a number on their shirt. The number is on the front and on the back. This way, the referee knows each player.
Look at these examples.
1. In a rally, players must not catch the ball.
2. Players must have a number on their shirt.
3. Players must not throw the ball.
4. The server must hit the ball with one hand or arm.
5. The serve must go over the net.

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: Work with a partner and tell the team's story. One partner tells the team's plans with be going to. This partner also talks about quick choices in a game with will. The other partner explains three volleyball rules with have to and must. Use don't have to and must not too. Then change jobs.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Now you can talk about plans, quick choices and rules on the volleyball court.

items.prompt: What are you going to do before your next big test or game?
What do you have to do at school? What don't you have to do?
Which volleyball rule surprised you most, and why?
